Today, we're going to talk about pesticide application - but a specific type of it. I imagine it's valuable to anyone who's interested in spray applications and it's also valid for those of you with smaller gardens.

My garden is pretty large. Like, unbelievably large - for a garden. My garden is approximately two acres of grow-space. That's just about two American gridiron football fields, with their end zones.

Unfortunately, it's too small to use a tractor and too big to actually use a small spray bottle.

The question is, how do I apply pesticides, why, and what?

The first question should be why do I apply pesticides? The short and snarky answer is to control pests - but that's actually pretty important. See, it's futile to apply pesticides if you don't actually know what pests you're defending against.

I'm also going to assume that we don't want complicated and we don't want expensive. So, rather than fret about a bunch of different types of pests, I'm just going to go ahead and recommend one - that's pretty universal. It is a little expensive but it's not very expensive and it's significantly cheaper if you buy in bulk.

So, get out there and get your hands dirty and see what kind of pests you have found. There's countless forums where you can submit a picture of your pest and you'll get a learned response telling you what kind of pest you're facing. If that fails, you're local State university has an agricultural extension (probably). Don't be afraid to approach academia - academia is pretty open to helping at no cost. They want to share their knowledge.

If you do decide to approach academia - do NOT bring a sample pest into them unless asked. Capture your pest, put it in a jar (with some of the food it was eating) and cover the jar. Take pictures and note what type of plant it was on, the time of day, and the atmospheric conditions. DO NOT BRING IN A PEST SAMPLE - unless you've been specifically asked to do so.

So, now you know what your pest is and you've done some research and found some strange chemical that's sure to rid yourself of the pest. You've read the MSDS and got the appropriate PPE and have ordered up your favorite batch of chemical soup to spray...

Skip that...

Citrus is horrible tasting. Both bugs and four legged critters don't like it any more than you do. No, an orange doesn't taste like citrus, really. An orange peel tastes like citrus. Citrus is bitter and not very tasty - so animals aren't really fond of it.

What I do, is I get the giant 5 gallon pail of this - one per season. I'm going to do something I don't normally do, and I'm going to recommend a specific brand - but you're free to find other brands. I'm just familiar with this brand and have had good luck since I started using it about 5 years ago.

https://www.factorydirectchemicals.com/products/cold-pressed-orange-oil

Like I said, I get the five gallon pail at my local(ish) garden store. You can probably find smaller bottles. I don't do the ground soaking. I just mix 2oz per gallon of water and apply it with something called an Indian Pump.

This is what an Indian Pump looks like:

https://imgoat.com/uploads/2ddea18f00/72569.jpg

You just fill 'er up (I've a hose that goes all the way to my garden - which is not an easy task for everyone) and lug it around and spray the plants. Don't worry, you can spray it on anything.

An Indian Pump comes with two nozzles, one will stream the liquid and the other will spray it. You'll want to take care to clean the nozzles out afterwards but it isn't very sticky or anything - not at that level of concentration.

It's safe - you can just drink it. It tastes like ass, but you can drink it.

Now, it's pretty effective for the pests that I get up here and is effective against a bunch of other pests. It's food-safe and rinses right off the veggies.

During the first month after planting, I apply the spray once every week. After the first month, I apply it every two weeks and I keep that up throughout the summer. It's so dilute that you'll find the rain (or your watering) washes it off to the point where you're unable to taste it - but the bugs can still taste it and they're really, really not fond of it.

You can use one of the small hand sprayers, a spray bottle, or even some sort of rag and a bowl of the stuff.

Some of the dirty hippies use a garlic concoction and it performs the same function - though that'd not work with me, 'cause I love garlic! (It's delicious!)

So, in wrap-up, use a concentrated citrus oil and make sure to dilute it properly. This works for most pests that I'm familiar with and will be easy enough for a garden your sizes. You can get an Indian Pump at your local hardware store, I have multiples 'cause we burn the blueberry fields. Clean your nozzles after each application, as it will be a wee bit sticky.

Now, go get some dirt under your fingernails and grow something!
